hints: Think about the difference between counting every atom present and simplifying to the smallest possible numbers that still keep the same proportion.
walkthrough:
Separate molecular from empirical**
Picture glucose, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$. That tells you the actual number of atoms. For empirical you divide everything down by the biggest common factor, here 6, to get $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$. You are keeping the proportion but using the smallest integers possible.
Final answer: The simplest whole number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.

hints: Keep the total at 5 carbons and only rings plus alkyl side chains, no C=C double bond, and remember cyclopentane and isomer C are already used.
Try a 4-membered ring with one carbon outside, then a 3-membered ring with two carbons outside in different arrangements.
walkthrough:
Count what must stay constant**
You need $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ and the structure must be cyclic. Cyclopentane uses a 5-membered ring with no side chain. Isomer C is 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane, a 3-membered ring with two methyl groups. So your new isomers must still total 5 carbons but be different skeletons.

Build the 4-membered option**
Take cyclobutane, a square, and attach one $\text{CH}_3$ group to one corner. That is methylcyclobutane: $4 + 1 = 5$ carbons. It is clearly different from a 5-membered ring and from a dimethyl 3-membered ring.

Build the 3-membered options**
Take cyclopropane, a triangle. You have two carbons left to add. Put them together as one ethyl group, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, to make ethylcyclopropane. Or put them as two separate methyl groups on the same carbon to make 1,1-dimethylcyclopropane. Either counts as a correct different isomer.
Final answer: Any two of: methylcyclobutane; ethylcyclopropane; 1,1-dimethylcyclopropane; 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane (cis or trans) drawn as skeletal structures.

hints: Recall what happens in initiation with UV light when $\text{Cl}_2$ forms two $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ radicals with one electron going to each atom.
walkthrough:
Picture the electrons splitting evenly**
In $\text{Cl}_2$, the shared pair could split unevenly to give ions, or evenly to give radicals. UV light causes one electron to go to each $\text{Cl}$ atom, forming two $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ radicals. Equal sharing of the pair means homolytic fission.
Final answer: Homolytic fission.

hints: In the first propagation a $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ removes H from cyclopentane, so think what two products must form when $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ loses one H.
In the second propagation the new carbon radical reacts with $\text{Cl}_2$ to make the organic chloride, so think what radical must be regenerated to keep the chain going.
walkthrough:
Follow the chain idea**
Propagation means a radical is used up and a new radical is made, so the chain continues. You start propagation 1 with $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10} + \text{Cl}^\bullet$.

Write propagation 1 as H abstraction**
$\text{Cl}^\bullet$ is very reactive and pulls a H atom off cyclopentane. Cyclopentane becomes $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9^\bullet$ and the H joins Cl to give $\text{HCl}$: $$\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10} + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_9^\bullet + \text{HCl}$$

Write propagation 2 as Cl transfer**
Now $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9^\bullet$ attacks a $\text{Cl}_2$ molecule. It takes one Cl to form the product $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$ and kicks out a fresh $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ to start the cycle again: $$\text{C}_5\text{H}_9^\bullet + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl} + \text{Cl}^\bullet$$

Final answer: propagation 1: $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10} + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_9^\bullet + \text{HCl}$
propagation 2: $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9^\bullet + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl} + \text{Cl}^\bullet$

hints: Think about what it means when two radicals join to make a stable molecule and no new radical is produced.
walkthrough:
Spot the end of the chain**
Look at $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9^\bullet + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$. Two radicals collide and pair their single electrons to make a normal covalent bond. Because no radical remains, the chain cannot continue. That is exactly what termination means.
Final answer: Termination.

hints: Compare cyclopentene and chlorocyclopentane and notice that H and Cl have added across the C=C double bond.
walkthrough:
Read reaction 3 as an addition**
Cyclopentene has a C=C bond and the product is chlorocyclopentane with one Cl on the ring. To convert C=C to H-C-C-Cl you need to add $\text{H}$ and $\text{Cl}$ across the double bond. The clean reagent for that is hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl(g)}$.

hints: Write the Hess expression for reaction 1, cyclopentene plus $\text{H}_2$ forming cyclopentane, as sum of combustion of reactants minus combustion of products.
Use the triangle in Fig. 3.2 to link reaction 2 to reaction 1 and reaction 3, noting that reaction 2 equals reaction 3 minus reaction 1.
walkthrough:
Calculate $\Delta H_1$ from combustion data**
For any reaction, $\Delta H_r = \Sigma \Delta H_c(\text{reactants}) - \Sigma \Delta H_c(\text{products})$ because combustion products are the common level. Reaction 1 is cyclopentene + $\text{H}_2 \rightarrow$ cyclopentane: $$\Delta H_1 = [(-3115) + (-286)] - [(-3292)]$$ $$\Delta H_1 = -3401 + 3292 = -109 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ This makes sense, hydrogenation of a C=C bond is exothermic.

Apply Hess law around the triangle**
Going from cyclopentane to chlorocyclopentane directly is reaction 2. The indirect route is backwards through reaction 1 to cyclopentene then forwards through reaction 3. So: $$\Delta H_2 = -\Delta H_1 + \Delta H_3$$ $$\Delta H_2 = -(-109) + (-53) = +109 - 53 = +56 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Reaction 2 is slightly endothermic.

Final answer: reaction 1: $\Delta H_1 = -3115 + (-286) - (-3292) = -109$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
$\Delta H_2 = \Delta H_3 - \Delta H_1 = -53 - (-109) = +56$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Remember hot concentrated acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ breaks the C=C bond completely and oxidises each C of the double bond to a carboxylic acid group.
walkthrough:
Open the ring at the double bond**
Imagine cyclopentene as a 5-membered ring with one C=C. Hot concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-/\text{H}^+$ does not just add OH, it cleaves the double bond open. Each of the two alkene carbons becomes a $-\text{COOH}$ carbon. The other three $\text{CH}_2$ groups stay linked in a chain.

Write the straight chain diacid**
Joining it up gives $\text{HOOC}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$, which has formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_8\text{O}_4$. That matches W exactly, so W is pentanedioic acid.
Final answer: $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ (pentanedioic acid).

hints: Look at Table 3.3 and find which bonds exist in a dicarboxylic acid W but cannot exist in the alkene cyclopentene.
Match the very broad absorption around $3000$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ and the strong sharp absorption around $1700$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ to those bonds.
walkthrough:
List what is new in W**
Cyclopentene has only C-H, C-C and C=C bonds. W has two $-\text{COOH}$ groups, so it introduces O-H (carboxyl type) and C=O bonds. Those must give new peaks.

Assign the broad $3000$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ dip**
In Fig. 3.3 the deep broad trough centred near $3000$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ matches the $2500-3000$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ range for O-H in a carboxyl group in Table 3.3. Label this as 1, bond responsible O-H.

Assign the strong $1720$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ dip**
The very strong sharp absorption near $1720$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ falls in the $1670-1740$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ range for C=O in carboxyl. Label this as 2, bond responsible C=O. Neither peak appears for cyclopentene.

Final answer: Absorption 1 at approx. $3000$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ (broad, $2500-3000$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$) due to O-H in carboxyl.
Absorption 2 at approx. $1720$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$ ($1670-1740$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$) due to C=O in carboxyl.
